The Car Industry Has a Seat-Belt Problem It Can’t Fix
 
Plus, Jensen Huang’s vision for the new Nvidia is a lot like the old one, and our game tests whether you can secure your money for old age
 
 
OCTAVIAN LAZAR/ALAMY
 

1. FROM MY DESK

 

The auto industry has spent billions of dollars to protect occupants in car crashes in recent decades. Yet all the air bags, cameras and emergency-braking systems in today’s cars fall short against one intractable hazard: the roughly 10% of people who still refuse to wear seat belts.

 

About 10,000 people die in U.S. crashes each year while unbuckled—about half of all occupant fatalities—a toll unchanged for over a decade.

 

New cars today are built safer than ever before. Yet, as Ryan Felton reports, that hasn’t meaningfully reduced roadway fatalities largely tied to three persistent problems: speeding, drunken driving and seat-belt misuse.

 

To get more drivers buckled up, industry leaders and regulators are revisiting an idea once so hated that Congress outlawed it a half-century ago.

 

A quick housekeeping note: We will be off tomorrow and Friday for Thanksgiving and back in your inboxes on Saturday.

 

This is an edition of The 10-Point newsletter, a guided tour of the best coverage in The Wall Street Journal. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here. If you’re reading this in your inbox, tap the headline above for online and audio versions of this newsletter.

 
 
 

2. TODAY’S HEADLINES

 

• The belief from Wall Street to the White House that Jensen Huang is uniquely qualified to lead Nvidia enabled his stunning return to the chip maker. Now, he has to prove his backers right.

 

• What would happen to the U.S. economy if the AI boom goes bust? It would take a painful hit, but the magnitude of the fallout remains a live debate.

 

• Democrats are already watering down their Medicare for All plans.

• Venezuela’s interim authorities disclosed that the country’s national debt load is $237 billion, a significantly higher-than-expected figure that underscores the financial challenges facing the U.S.-backed government.

4. READ IT HERE FIRST

 

Jamie Dimon loved Britain, until it raised taxes on JPMorgan.

 

Jamie Dimon is such a professed Anglophile that he threw a birthday party in King Charles III’s name last year and made sure JPMorgan Chase’s new Manhattan skyscraper has an English pub. But his love affair with Britain has hit a rocky patch over the Labour government’s plans to raise taxes on banks, report Alexander Saeedy and Joe Wallace. The levy hike irked Dimon, whose bank estimates it will pay an extra £120 million over the 15 months in which the tax is supposed to remain in place. The longtime banker is seeking to strike back against the U.K. as a way to warn other governments against making life harder for businesses, according to people familiar with his thinking.

 

5.

 

Shapiro accuses Biden of not doing enough to rein in Netanyahu.

 

Josh Shapiro hasn’t announced a presidential run for 2028, but he is sounding a starting gun on what is likely to be a fractious debate over foreign policy in the Democratic primaries. The Pennsylvania governor’s stance on Israel will face particular scrutiny if he enters the presidential primary, as the Democratic Party grows more divided over its relationship with the country. In an interview with Robbie Gramer, Shapiro defended the U.S.-Israel alliance while saying there needs to be accountability for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s actions in Gaza. He said neither former President Joe Biden nor President Trump took sufficient steps to constrain Netanyahu during the Gaza war.
